title: How Bees Make Honey
source: Original passage written for this demonstration (no ReadWorks content)
content:
A spoonful of honey tastes sweet and simple, but it takes an enormous team of insects to make it. Honey bees work together all summer long, and every bee has a job.

The story begins with a worker bee leaving the hive to look for flowers. When she finds one, she uses her long, thin tongue to drink the nectar, a sugary liquid inside the flower. She stores the nectar in a special stomach called the honey stomach. This stomach is separate from the one she uses to digest her own food.

A single bee may visit dozens, or even hundreds, of flowers on one trip. As she goes from flower to flower, grains of pollen stick to her fuzzy body. Some of the pollen falls off at the next flower, which helps the plants make seeds and fruit. In this way, bees do two important things at once: they collect food, and they help plants grow.

When her honey stomach is full, the bee flies home. Inside the hive, she passes the nectar to a younger worker bee. That bee chews the nectar for a while, mixing it with natural substances from her body that change its sugars. Then she places the nectar in a small wax cell.

At this point, the nectar is still thin and watery. To turn it into honey, the bees must remove most of the water. Hundreds of workers stand near the cells and fan their wings. The moving air makes the water evaporate. After several days, the liquid becomes thick and sticky. Fresh nectar is mostly water, but finished honey has only about one-sixth water in it.

Once the honey is ready, the bees seal the cell with a thin cap of wax. The honey stays safe inside, like food in a jar. During the winter, when there are no flowers, the bees eat the honey to stay alive and warm.

Making honey takes huge amounts of work. One worker bee makes only about one-twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her whole life. To fill a single jar, the bees of a hive must visit millions of flowers.

Bees also have a clever way to share information. A bee that finds a good patch of flowers returns to the hive and dances. The dance, which scientists call the waggle dance, tells the other bees which direction to fly and how far to go.

The next time you taste honey, remember the thousands of small travelers behind it. Each spoonful is the result of many bees, many flowers, and many busy summer days.
